research_concepts: adherence to recommended offensive play-type mix
methodological_questions: How to define a suppression-conditional recommended mix from suppressor profiles
How to measure adherence of observed play-type mix to the recommended mix
Whether series-level sample (n=54) provides adequate power
How to control for team-quality confounding
Whether suppressor-profile instability affects measurement reliability
Whether regression-to-the-mean artifacts inflate apparent strategic effects

historical_evidence.finding: RTM (ppp_h1 alone) explains 32.9% of second-half PPP collapse variance; usage, process/shot-zone, lineup, and context add only ~1.7 pp, with 65.4% unexplained idiosyncratic noise. No strong strategic effect beyond RTM.
PUTBACK is the top sequential suppressor for 6+ stars (e.g. D. Mitchell -0.294 PPP, n_after=95), but no multiplicity correction; other play types have small counts. Descriptive only.

Rank-1 suppressor varies meaningfully across players (e.g. Jokic after opp POST_UP -0.0675, SE ±0.0500, n=480), but deltas mostly within 1-2 SE with no multiple-comparison control; OTHER artifact flagged.
First-half usage does not predict second-half suppression after controlling for H1 PPP/RTM (ATT = +0.0313, BH p=0.0658 weak; predictive lift over mean reversion only +0.039). RTM dominates.
Games where a team's play-type mix is closer to the model's recommended mix produce +5.18 raw ORtg and +3.27 strength-controlled ORtg improvement. Model regret median +25.94 ORtg.
Single-game descriptive conformance scoring (ORL vs DET) showing leverage-weighted mix deviations. No outcome comparison.
Teams' observed play-type mix often does not match the recommended opener (average |delta| 4.5–24.0 pp), but single-game scope and no outcome test.
Series-level AVOID share rho=-0.26, p=0.07 (n=50 series, ~80 needed for p<0.05). Confounded by team quality (low AVOID teams are often good teams).
Only 2/30 (7%) stars have the same top sequential suppressor in ≥75% of seasons; sequential suppression is unstable across years.
Non-CUT BEST vs feasibility-weighted league mix: gap +0.010 PPP, p=0.1709 (n=136); H2H L3 non-CUT gap +0.001, p=0.3277. Strategic edge outside CUT is negligible.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Series-level test of strategic share predicting winning
failed_approaches.why: n=50 series underpowered; need ~80 for p<0.05; team quality confound persisted even after binning.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Using first-half usage to predict second-half suppression
failed_approaches.why: Effect was WEAK/NULL after Benjamini-Hochberg correction; predictive lift over mean reversion only +0.039.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Variance decomposition of H1→H2 PPP collapse to find strategic triggers
failed_approaches.why: Process/usage/lineup/context added only ~1.7 percentage points beyond regression to the mean.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Testing stability of sequential suppressors across seasons
failed_approaches.why: Only 2 of 30 stars met the stability threshold; suppressors are unstable, undermining recommendations conditioned on them.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Testing non-CUT matchup-specific BEST counters vs league mix
failed_approaches.why: Non-CUT gap +0.010, p=0.1709; the only robust advantage came from CUT plays.

evidence_establishes: Adherence to a (non-suppression-conditional) recommended mix improves offensive efficiency (SF-APPM-001).
Series-level tests of strategic adherence predicting winning suffer from small sample and talent confounding (SF-CHT-039).
Second-half suppression is dominated by regression to the mean, leaving little room for observable strategic effects (SF-APPS-076, SF-APPS-070).
Sequential-suppressor identities are unstable across seasons (SF-APPA-058) and estimated with wide uncertainty (SF-APPM-022).
Non-CUT strategic advantages are small and often indistinguishable from noise (SF-APPS-023).
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether a suppression-conditional recommended mix specifically predicts series wins.
That the positive efficiency effect in SF-APPM-001 translates into a detectable win-probability gain at the series level (n=54).
That suppressors can be identified with enough precision and stability to form actionable, generalisable recommendations.
That the effect size of adherence is large enough to overcome RTM, team-quality confounding, and small-series power.
own_inferences: Defining a 'suppression-conditional recommended mix' requires robust suppressor profiles, which the current evidence base does not provide (APPM-022 inconclusive, APPA-058 stability null).
If a recommended mix is constructed, adherence likely mirrors the positive PPP effects found in APPM-001, but the win impact at series level would be small and easily swamped by talent differences.
With only 54 series, even a moderate correlation would not reach conventional significance, as CHT-039's nearly identical setup demonstrates.
Measurement error from unstable suppressor profiles will attenuate any true association, further reducing power.
A game-level analysis could increase sample size but would introduce within-series dependencies and still face confounding.
uncertainties: The exact definition of 'suppression-conditional recommended mix' is not specified; a more reliable operationalisation using stable, pooled suppressor estimates might improve measurement.
If more seasons of data were available (e.g., aggregating several years), series count could increase, mitigating the power problem.
No study has directly tested the conditional variant of the recommended mix against winning; the closest is APPM-001 (efficiency) and CHT-039 (AVOID share).
Whether the 2025-26 season (partial) and playoffs could supplement series count is unclear.

historical_effect.explanation: Without the historical evidence, the question might appear testable with the series data. The retrieval revealed that a nearly identical design (SF-CHT-039) failed due to small sample and confounding, that suppressor profiles are unstable (SF-APPA-058) and inconclusive (SF-APPM-022), and that strategic effects beyond RTM are tiny (SF-APPS-076, SF-APPS-070). These findings collectively indicate that a test with 54 series is very unlikely to succeed, so the decision changed from a potential proceed to do_not_proceed.

blocking_constraints.text: With only 54 series, the design is underpowered; SF-CHT-039 required ~80 series for a medium effect, and the anticipated adherence effect is likely smaller.
Team quality confounds both adherence (better teams may follow recommendations more closely) and winning; residual-based controls are difficult with a small series sample.

Suppressor profiles are unstable (SF-APPA-058) and estimated with large uncertainty (SF-APPM-022). A recommended mix built on such noisy inputs will contain substantial measurement error, attenuating any true signal.
Regression to the mean dominates second-half performance changes; apparent adherence effects may be artefacts of selecting series with extreme first-half outcomes.

prior_work.summary: SF-APPM-001 shows that mix alignment improves efficiency, but does not use a suppression-conditional model and does not test winning. SF-CHT-039 demonstrates that a series-level test of strategic share against winning is underpowered and confounded. SF-APPS-076 and SF-APPA-058 weaken the foundations for building a reliable suppression-conditional recommendation. Together, these partly address the required components and expose key obstacles, but the exact research question has not been directly tested.

risks.text: n = 54 series is insufficient to detect a plausible win-probability effect of adherence; prior analog required ~80 series for a larger expected effect.
Team talent is a likely confounder (good teams win more and may adhere better). Controlling for regular-season record or net rating shrinks residual degrees of freedom further.
The recommended mix depends on estimated suppressors; those estimates are unstable (SF-APPA-058) and have wide standard errors (SF-APPM-022), introducing attenuation bias.
If series are selected based on extreme half-to-half shifts, the adherence effect may be confounded by regression to the mean, as documented in SF-APPS-076 and SF-APPS-070.
Any exploration of alternative adherence metrics, time windows, or model specifications would require a multiplicity correction that the small sample cannot support.

design.estimand: The difference in series win probability associated with a one-unit increase in average adherence to a suppression-conditional recommended mix, controlling for team strength.
design.sample: All available playoff series from 2022-23 through 2025-26. With 54 series this yields low power; minimum viable design would require at least 4–5 additional playoff seasons (>80 series).
design.power: Assuming a medium point-biserial correlation r=0.30 between adherence and series win, n=54 provides power ~0.35; to reach 0.80, approximately 85–90 series are needed. Anticipated true effect likely smaller (r ~0.15), requiring over 300 series.
design.controls: Pre-series team strength (regular-season net rating, SRS, or a Bayesian talent estimate) entered as a covariate. Sensitivity analysis modelling the effect unadjusted and with opponent strength.
design.falsification: Within the same design, test a placebo exposure: preceding-series adherence (adherence from a series that concluded before the current opponent) should not predict win; time-stratified randomisation of adherence within team-seasons to detect artificial structure.
design.multiplicity: All analyses pre-registered with a single primary adherence metric (e.g., L1 distance averaged over series games) and a single outcome (series win). Any exploratory metrics reported as secondary with full disclosure.
design.decision_rule: One-tailed test of positive association between adherence and win probability, alpha=0.05, using logistic regression or permuted exact test. Present effect estimate with 95% confidence interval. Do not claim support if confidence interval includes zero or if placebo test fails.
design.data_version: NBA 2022-23 to 2025-26 playoffs, play-by-play derived play-type possessions and matchup data, locked before analysis. If proceeding, data would be extended to include additional historical seasons.

methodological_questions: how to define adherence to a recommended mix
how to define suppression-conditional recommended mix
causal inference from observational play-by-play data
lookahead bias in strategy adherence measurement
small sample size with series as units

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- explore_graph(node_id): the relationships of one graph node (a family or a question, method, dataset, measure, limitation or risk node), with neighbour labels.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

Research question (as posed on 2026-06-16, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
Adhering to a suppression-conditional recommended mix predicts winning.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 54 series

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

Stage 1. Reply only with the retrieval call: {"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["..."], "methodological_questions": ["..."], "query": "..."}}

reasoning_details.text:
We are in stage 1: retrieval. We need to read the research question and data description, identify research concepts and methodological questions, then call retrieve_history.

Research question: "Adhering to a suppression-conditional recommended mix predicts winning." The area is defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid). The data: per-game NBA data from multiple seasons, with play-by-play, substitutions, defensive matchups, box-score, derived play-type possession records in a graph database. Units available: 54 series (likely playoff series? but also regular season? "series" might refer to playoff series - but data includes regular seasons too. The question uses "suppression-conditional recommended mix" - probably refers to a previously defined suppression strategy or counter strategy mix. This seems related to defensive suppression: maybe a defensive strategy that aims to suppress the opponent's scoring, and a "recommended mix" of actions (maybe play types, lineup choices) that depends on the opponent's tendencies (conditional). The question is whether adhering to that mix predicts winning. So we need to identify research concepts: "suppression-conditional recommended mix", "adherence", "winning" (outcome). Methodological questions: How to define adherence? How to define the recommended mix? How to measure winning? Causal identification? Confounders? Potential lookahead bias? Series-level analysis? Also, the data: per-game but units are 54 series; maybe the study is at series level, so winning a series. But we have per-game data, so could aggregate. Risks: multiple testing, overfitting, small sample (54 series), mechanical floor, etc.

Let's call retrieve_history with appropriate research concepts and methodological questions.

Research concepts: "suppression-conditional recommended mix", "defensive suppression", "counter strategy", "adherence to strategy", "winning". But we can be more concise: the core is adherence to a recommended defensive/strategic mix under suppression conditions. Might be related to previous families like "defensive gameplay adjustments", "strategic adherence", "play-type mix". We'll infer from the domain: this project has likely studied similar topics. So we'll list concepts like "defensive suppression strategy", "counter strategy", "recommended mix adherence", "winning prediction".

Methodological questions: "how to define adherence", "how to define recommended mix", "confounding", "causal inference from observational data", "small sample size", "lookahead bias", "measurement of suppression conditional".

Query string: "adhering to a suppression-conditional recommended mix predicts winning"

Let's craft the call.

We start stage 2. The retrieval returned several study families. We need to parse each record, extract historical evidence and failed approaches exactly as recorded. Use only identifiers from the retrieved list. Let's go through each record and note its status, findings, failure evidence if any, and whether it relates to the current research question. The current question is: "Adhering to a suppression-conditional recommended mix predicts winning." This means we have some definition of a "recommended mix" that is conditional on suppression (presumably the opponent's defensive suppression strategy), and we want to test if teams that adhere to that recommended mix (in terms of their offensive play-type mix) are more likely to win.

We need to assess testability, risks, etc., and produce the final output.

First, identify research concepts and methodological questions from the question.

Research concepts:
- Defensive suppression
- Counter strategy / recommended mix
- Adherence to a mix
- Suppression-conditional recommended mix
- Winning prediction

Methodological questions:
- How to define suppression-conditional recommended mix? (e.g., what is the model that outputs a recommended mix given the opponent's suppression profile?)
- How to measure adherence? (E.g., distance between actual mix and recommended mix)
- What is the outcome: winning (binary win/loss, or point differential)?
- Unit of analysis: 54 series available? The question mentions "Adhering to a suppression-conditional recommended mix predicts winning." The data description says "Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 54 series". So presumably we are looking at playoff series. So the unit might be a series. Winning at the series level? Or game level aggregated to series? "Predicts winning" could be series outcome or game win. The units are series, so likely series-level analysis. That raises sample size concerns (54 series). Also strategic adherence might vary game-to-game, but aggregated over series, so we have a small N.

Now examine the retrieved families.

1. FAM:SF-APPS-076: "Trigger attribution: variance of H1->H2 PPP collapse". Status: rejected (observed_outcome_status). Finding: RTM explains 32.9% of variance; usage, process, lineup, context add ~1.7 pp; residual 65.4%. This is about explaining suppression triggers (i.e., why teams' performance drops from first half to second half). It is about variance decomposition, not directly about recommended mix adherence and winning. But it relates to suppression and RTM dominance. Might inform methodological risk: RTM is strong, making strategic explanations hard. Failed approach: powered null result, showing that process/usage/lineup/context add little beyond RTM. So this suggests that strategic variables (like mix adherence) might have small effect sizes, making it hard to detect winning impact.

2. FAM:SF-APPA-050: "Superstar sequential suppression: opponent play before the star". Status: not a hypothesis test. Describes that specific opponent play types suppress star PPP on next possession. Not directly about recommended mix adherence. Could be relevant for defining suppression-conditional recommended mix: if we can identify which play types suppress a given opponent's star, then we could recommend mix based on that. But this study is descriptive, no multiplicity correction. Failed approach: E_unclear. Small n_after cells. This is a piece of evidence about sequential suppression.

3. FAM:SF-APPM-022: "Superstar suppression profiles (incl. Q5c sequential triggering)". Status: inconclusive. Findings: rank-1 suppressor varies across players, but deltas mostly within 1-2 SE, no multiplicity control, OTHER artifact flagged. This is about identifying top suppressors for stars. Could be used to define suppression-conditional recommended mix, but the evidence is weak. Failure mechanism: E_unclear, no multiple-comparison control. So not a reliable basis for defining recommendations.

4. FAM:SF-APPS-070: "H1 usage as predictor of H2 suppression (distribution shift)". Status: rejected. Finding: first-half usage does not predict second-half suppression after controlling for H1 PPP/RTM. So again RTM dominates. Not directly about recommended mix adherence predicting winning, but about predicting suppression from usage. This might be relevant if the recommended mix is based on usage patterns; but it's about predicting suppression, not winning. Failure: B_powered_null.

5. FAM:SF-APPM-001: "Play-type mix alignment vs actual PPP (matchup residual)". Status: supported. Finding: holdout games where team's play-type mix is closer to the model's recommended mix score more efficiently (strength-controlled gap +3.27 ORtg). This is directly relevant! The recommended mix here is not explicitly "suppression-conditional", but likely matchup-based. The study shows alignment with recommended mix yields higher offensive efficiency. However, it doesn't test winning directly. But it's a closely related concept: adherence to recommended mix improves offensive efficiency, which likely helps winning. But the research question is specifically "suppression-conditional recommended mix", which might be a subset or different from the model's recommended mix in APPM-001. Need to examine details. The attributes: "Raw gap aligned-deviated +5.18 ORtg; strength-controlled gap +3.27 ORtg (+0.0193 vs -0.0134 PPP residual). Model regret median +25.94 ORtg (non-negative by construction)." It says supported, n=908 rows (game-team rows), no CI stated. This is a positive result, but again not about winning directly. Could be considered evidence that mix alignment improves PPP. Winning is a function of PPP differential. So this might partially answer the question. But the question says "adhering to a suppression-conditional recommended mix predicts winning." This study is about a recommended mix, but is it suppression-conditional? The abstract mentions "matchup residual", so it likely incorporates opponent defensive characteristics. That might be considered suppression-conditional. So it provides some support. The fact that it is supported is important. So this could be prior work that partly answers the question, but maybe not explicitly with winning as outcome. We'll note that.

6. FAM:SF-APPA-032: "Execution conformance scoring ORL vs DET". Status: not a hypothesis test. Single-game descriptive. Not directly relevant.

7. FAM:SF-APPS-017: "Execution conformance of observed mix vs recommended plan". Status: not a hypothesis test. Single-game, no outcome comparison, descriptive. Not directly about winning. Shows that teams often do not follow the recommended opener exactly. Could be relevant for adherence measurement but not for win prediction.

8. FAM:SF-CHT-039: "Series-level AVOID share vs winning (talent confound)". Status: untestable. Finding: game-level negative correlation (higher AVOID share losing), but series-level rho=-0.26 p=0.07 underpowered (n=50 series). Confounded by team quality. This is directly relevant because it's about adherence to a strategy (AVOID share) predicting winning at series level. Here, AVOID is a different strategy concept (probably avoiding bad play types). The question is about adherence to a recommended mix, but similar methodological issues: small series sample size, confounding by talent. So this provides strong lessons: series-level analysis with 50 series leads to underpowered and confounded. This is the most directly analogous study. So we must cite it heavily. It suggests that testing "adherence to X predicts winning" at series level is challenging. So this is a key failed approach.

9. FAM:SF-APPA-058: "Season stability of top suppressors and negative teammate pairs". Status: rejected. Only 2/30 stable top suppressors across seasons. This suggests that suppression-conditional recommendations might not be stable, which could impact the test if the definition of "suppression-conditional recommended mix" relies on stable suppressors.

10. FAM:SF-APPS-023: "System BEST vs constrained league mix (non-CUT matchup-specificity test)". Status: rejected. Finding: non-CUT BEST vs mix gap +0.010 p=0.1709, so null. This is about BEST vs mix, not directly about winning, but shows that non-CUT (i.e., non-cut related) strategic advantages are small. This might be relevant because suppression-conditional recommended mix might be a type of BEST counter. But again not about winning.

Now, we need to synthesize: The research question's testability. The unit is series (54 series). We need to define "suppression-conditional recommended mix": likely based on models from the project that output recommended play-type mix for a given opponent's defensive suppression profile. Adherence could be measured as distance (L1, etc.) between actual mix and recommended mix aggregated over games within a series. Winning is series outcome (binary) or maybe win probability? Could be series win/loss. So we are testing whether the average (or sum of) adherence across games in a series is correlated/associated with series win, controlling for team quality and other factors. With 54 series, power is limited, as CHT-039 shows ~80 series needed for p<0.05 for a similar association. The effect size for recommended mix adherence might be even smaller than AVOID share. Also confounding by team quality: good teams both win more and may have better adherence (or may not need to adhere as much because they are good anyway). So confounded. Additionally, defining suppression-conditional recommended mix may rely on uncertain suppressor identifications (as APPM-022 and APPA-058 show instability). So the recommended mix might be noisy, leading to measurement error and attenuation bias. Also RTM effects could dominate, making strategic effects small.

So testability seems low. p_testable might be around 0.2-0.3? Let's quantify: given small sample (54 series), likely small effect size, confounding, measurement unreliability, prior null results on related questions. We need to provide blocking constraints: SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, CONFOUNDING, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, etc.

Now we need to produce historical_evidence list: for each relevant record, we include its id, status_as_recorded, and finding summarized. But we should only include records that are relevant to the research question. We can include all 10 as they all have some relevance, but we must ensure consistency. The schema says "historical_evidence" list of objects with id and status and finding. We'll list all returned records except perhaps the ones that are completely irrelevant? But we can include them all, as the retrieval returned them. However, we should focus on those that inform the decision. The instructions: "keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference". So we'll create list with all 10? That's fine.

Failed_approaches: list those that represent failed approaches relevant to the research question. Specifically, SF-CHT-039 is untestable due to small sample and confounding; that is a clear failed approach for series-level adherence predicting winning. SF-APPS-070 and SF-APPS-076 show that strategic variables add little beyond RTM, failing to find effects. SF-APPS-023 failed to reject null for non-CUT BEST. SF-APPA-058 showed instability of suppressors, which would affect reliability. So we can list several.

Evidence_establishes: from the evidence, we can say: Adherence to a recommended mix (non-suppression-conditional) improves offensive efficiency (APPM-001). Series-level analog (AVOID share vs winning) is underpowered and confounded (CHT-039). Suppression triggers are mostly RTM with little strategic effect (APPS-076, APPS-070). Suppressor identification is unstable across seasons (APPA-058) and inconclusive (APPM-022). So overall, the necessary components for a suppression-conditional recommended mix are weak.

Evidence_does_not_establish: whether a suppression-conditional recommended mix specifically predicts winning; the APPM-001 result does not use suppression-conditional model, and winning outcome is not directly tested. The instability of suppressors suggests the conditional recommendations may be unreliable.

Own_inferences: the test would face many challenges; effect sizes likely small; power insufficient; confounding. We'll detail.

uncertainties: how exactly the suppression-conditional recommended mix would be derived; whether any new data or model improvements could increase reliability; whether a game-level analysis pooling across series could improve power but then autocorrelation and unit of analysis issues.

historical_effect: changed_decision? We need to see if historical evidence changes our prior decision. Without the evidence, we might think it's plausible. With evidence, we see that related attempts (CHT-039) failed due to sample size, and underlying suppressor instability and RTM dominance make it unlikely. So probably changed decision to do_not_proceed. But we can state that.

testability: p_testable low, say 0.2. Blocking constraints: SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER (54 series is too few), CONFOUNDING (team quality), MEASURE_RELIABILITY (suppressor instability), RTM_SELECTION (mean reversion may confound adherence), etc.

prior_work: already_answered? Partly, by APPM-001 (efficiency connection) and CHT-039 (series-level prediction). But not the specific question. So "partly". Cite those.

risks: list with codes and text.

predicted_outcome: likely untestable or rejected. We'll assign probabilities: supported low, rejected medium, untestable high, artifact low, uncertain low. For instance: supported 0.1, rejected 0.3, untestable 0.5, artifact 0.05, uncertain 0.05. Sum to 1.

decision: do_not_proceed, but we could suggest proceed_with_changes if we change design (e.g., game-level analysis, more seasons, better suppressor definition). But with 54 series only, sample is fixed. So do_not_proceed.

design: provide a minimum viable test: would need >80 series, control for team strength, and validated suppressor profiles, etc. So design even if do_not_proceed.
